profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in a radiation oncology department to organize a small retrospective implementation-and-validation project for the Co-CRIM planning technique in Pinnacle for peripheral lung SBRT. The department wants to recreate the technique on 20 prior peripheral lung cases, compare it against existing CRT/IMRT/VMAT plans already stored in the TPS, and prepare a feasibility summary for an internal protocol review. The agenda is to decide which historical cases qualify, how the planners will build the Co-CRIM plans in Pinnacle, what 'comparison-ready' outputs need to be produced, who will handle planning versus physics review, and the timeline for completing the first batch. The expected outcome is an agreed work plan for case selection, planning setup, QA review, and a target date for the first interim dataset.

members.name: Dr. Lena Wu
members.expertise: Thoracic SBRT, protocol design, target/OAR evaluation
members.background: Attending radiation oncologist who leads thoracic case review and has previously published dosimetric comparisons in lung SBRT; she is comfortable with planning concepts but does not personally build plans in Pinnacle day to day.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, publication-quality retrospective dataset quickly, with cases that are easy to defend clinically and metrics that can be summarized without extensive replanning or re-contouring. She is also trying to avoid reopening old motion-management debates or introducing too many patient-specific exceptions.
hidden_assumptions: When a study says 'peripheral lung SBRT cases,' it naturally means the department's standard peripheral cohort already treated under current thoracic SBRT conventions, including the usual mix of 4D-CT derived ITV cases regardless of exact fractionation pattern.

Using the 'same constraints' across techniques means reusing the clinically approved organ-at-risk goals and target priorities already attached to each patient's final approved plan, not rebuilding a new uniform optimization template from scratch.

A plan being 'comparison-ready' means the key dosimetric table is complete from DVH outputs and physician review has confirmed target coverage and OAR acceptability; delivery QA can follow once the planning set looks stable.
The phrase 'first batch by next Friday' naturally refers to material ready for the Friday thoracic research meeting during normal clinic hours.

members.name: Evan Morales
members.expertise: Treatment planning systems, Pinnacle inverse optimization, patient-specific QA and dosimetric validation
members.background: Lead physicist for external beam planning workflow, responsible for Pinnacle configuration, plan normalization standards, and pre-treatment QA processes; he often translates published planning methods into reproducible departmental workflows.
members.private_state: He wants the recreation to be technically faithful to the published Co-CRIM method and auditable if the department later expands it into a formal methods paper. He is concerned that if the setup is too loosely defined, observed gains will reflect planning inconsistency rather than the technique itself.
hidden_assumptions: When replicating a published planning technique, 'peripheral lung SBRT cases' should be filtered into a tightly standardized cohort with the same prescription style and motion-management structure to avoid methodological noise.

Using the 'same constraints' means applying one common Pinnacle objective set and normalization rule across all recreated plans so the comparison isolates technique rather than legacy planner choices.

A plan is only truly 'comparison-ready' once it has passed the department's standard physics checks, including a deliverability-oriented review and gamma verification setup for the candidate technique.
The phrase 'first batch by next Friday' refers to files finalized in the research share by end of day Friday so physics can run its checks without meeting-time dependencies.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the peripheral lung cohort
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use '20 peripheral lung SBRT cases.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the usual departmental peripheral lung retrospective pool, including any clinically peripheral lesions treated with standard SBRT workflows, even if fractionation or planning-era conventions vary somewhat.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a narrower, methodologically uniform subset: peripheral lesions with closely matched prescription/fractionation patterns and planning structure so the Co-CRIM recreation is technically comparable case to case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe 'peripheral lung SBRT cases' is already a familiar category in the department, so it feels like a straightforward inclusion label rather than a boundary that needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of using the same constraints
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the Co-CRIM plans should be built with 'the same constraints' as the comparators.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means each patient's previously approved clinical target/OAR goals and physician expectations should be reused, preserving patient-specific constraints from the archived plans.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means all recreated plans should share one standardized optimization objective set and normalization convention in Pinnacle, even if that differs from what was used historically on a given patient.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning conversations, 'same constraints' sounds like obvious fairness language, and both parties assume the other is invoking the standard notion of methodological consistency.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have the first set of cases 'comparison-ready.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means dosimetric outputs and review notes are sufficient to compare techniques internally; QA is a downstream confirmation step.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the cases should already have physics-level readiness, including deliverability review and setup for gamma-based verification, before they count as ready for comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'comparison-ready' sounds operational rather than technical, and each person maps it onto their own stage of workflow without hearing a contradiction.

misalignment_points.topic: Interpretation of the Friday first-batch deadline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the first batch will be ready 'by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a physician-review packet prepared in time for the Friday thoracic research meeting, effectively by late morning or early afternoon local clinic time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects planning files uploaded by end of day Friday, after which he can complete physics-side checks and archive the batch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline phrases like 'by Friday' are routine shorthand, and because both think the timeline is reasonable, neither feels the need to specify the handoff moment or intended use that day.

That's the easiest dataset to defend internally and the easiest to extract without reopening old motion-management arguments.
